Logging to local or network paths detected
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\log4Net.xml

Explanation

Logging to local or network paths detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, prefer Application Insights/App Service logging. If filesystem logs are required, write to a mounted Azure Files share configured via storage mounts and Key Vault secrets.

Logging APIs that write to disk might not work on Azure App Service or Container.

Use logging that stores logs in locations outside of the host unless its specifically required by your app. You can also use logging capabilities embedded in Azure, such as Azure App Service logging or Application Insights.

For migrating to AKS, use LogMonitor tool that can capture logs written to files, the console, or write logs and redirect them to Azure.

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Global.asax.csLine 42

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Web.config

Explanation

Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move session to Azure Cache for Redis or Cosmos DB. In-proc session impedes scale-out; Managed Instance does not change session semantics.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

In-proc or local process stored session state not immediately prevents an application from working in Azure, however, is not recommended because it would make scaling the Azure App Service or Azure Kubernetes Service more difficult.

Azure provides multiple ways to store session state in a scalable way using Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Cosmos DB or other services.

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
eShopLegacy.Utilities\eShopLegacy.Utilities.csproj
eShopPorted\eShopPorted.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.

Deprecated Remoting & Serialization
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy .NET Remoting, BinaryFormatter, and related serialization APIs that are deprecated and removed for security reasons. Remoting provided distributed object communication but had significant security vulnerabilities. Migrate to gRPC, HTTP APIs, or modern serialization (System.Text.Json, protobuf).
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
ASP.NET Framework (System.Web)
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy ASP.NET Framework APIs for web applications (System.Web.*) that don't exist in ASP.NET Core due to architectural differences. ASP.NET Core represents a complete redesign of the web framework. Migrate to ASP.NET Core equivalents or consider System.Web.Adapters package for compatibility.

CVE-2024-21907: Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions in Newtonsoft.Json
 Mandatory 1
File
src/eShopLegacyMVC/eShopLegacyMVC.csproj:103
src/eShopLegacyMVC/packages.config:29

Explanation

CVE-2024-21907: Newtonsoft.Json versions before 13.0.1 can consume excessive CPU and memory or trigger a stack overflow when processing deeply nested JSON, potentially causing denial of service. Severity: HIGH.

Affected dependency: Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.1, declared in src/eShopLegacyMVC/eShopLegacyMVC.csproj and src/eShopLegacyMVC/packages.config. The other discovered declaration, Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.2, is not in the affected range.

Recommended fix: Upgrade the affected dependency to 13.0.1 or later. NuGet dependency-tree enumeration was unavailable because the legacy MVC project imports a missing Microsoft.WebApplication.targets; the scan therefore used declared direct dependencies only.

Data Storage & External Services

The legacy application is configured for SQL Server LocalDB and Entity Framework 6. The ported application has a separate LocalDB connection and EF Core model, but its checked-in settings enable mock data by default. No external APIs, message brokers, caches, or service-discovery systems were identified.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Both applications expose the same catalog domain through separate MVC/API and persistence stacks; they are not a distributed service system.
  • Autofac selects either a per-application mock catalog service or a database-backed service through the UseMockData setting.
  • The mock implementation is a singleton with mutable in-memory catalog state when enabled.

DTOs & Contracts

CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, and CatalogType are the domain/API model classes. PaginatedItemsViewModel packages paginated results for MVC responses. Each FilesController defines a nested BrandDTO with Id and Brand for its serialized response. The DTOs are mutable classes; no OpenAPI, protobuf, or GraphQL contracts were found. Standard MVC/Web API JSON serialization is used for JSON responses, while the files endpoints use the shared BinaryFormatter utility.

Communication Patterns

All service operations are synchronous local method calls from controllers to ICatalogService, then to EF6/EF Core or an in-memory mock. No inter-service REST clients, message brokers, retries, circuit breakers, service discovery, API gateway, or client-side load balancing were identified. There is no configured API authentication or authorization policy. Development launch profiles mention HTTPS, but no application-wide TLS enforcement was identified.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports browsing and maintaining a product catalog for an online shop. Catalog items are categorized by brand and product type and can be displayed with an associated image.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalogA sellable catalog entry with price, stock, and image metadataBelongs to one brand and one product type
CatalogBrandCatalogBrand identity used to group catalog productsCan be associated with multiple catalog items
CatalogTypeCatalogProduct classification such as mug or shirtCan be associated with multiple catalog items

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopLegacyMVCProduct CatalogCatalog items, brands, and typesLocal SQL Server database or in-memory mock
eShopPortedProduct CatalogCatalog items, brands, and typesSeparate LocalDB database or in-memory mock

The two applications implement the same catalog context independently. There is no cross-context data exchange or service-to-service ownership boundary.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse the catalog

  1. A client requests the catalog page with optional pagination values.
  2. The controller delegates to ICatalogService.
  3. The service retrieves a page of catalog items and attaches brand/type data, using EF or the configured mock implementation.
  4. The controller supplies image URI placeholders and renders a paginated view.

Workflow 2: Maintain catalog items

  1. An operator submits catalog item details through the create or edit form.
  2. Model binding and data annotations validate the submitted model.
  3. The controller calls CreateCatalogItem or UpdateCatalogItem; the service persists the change or updates the mock list.
  4. The application redirects to the catalog listing. Delete follows a similar controller/service path.

Workflow 3: Display a catalog image

  1. The client requests an image by catalog item identifier.
  2. PicController resolves the item through the catalog service.
  3. The controller reads the file named by the item's PictureFileName and returns it with an image MIME type.

Cross-Service Data Flows

No cross-service composition occurs. Each application obtains catalog items and related brand/type data from its own service implementation. In mock mode, data is supplied from in-memory preconfigured collections; in database mode, the application queries its own SQL database. The image flow is local to the same application and file system.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant Operator as "Catalog Operator" participant Controller as "Catalog Controller" participant Service as "Catalog Service" participant Database as "Catalog Database" Operator->>Controller: Submit catalog item Controller->>Controller: Validate model alt Input is valid Controller->>Service: Create or update item Service->>Database: Save catalog item Database-->>Service: Save result Service-->>Controller: Operation complete Controller-->>Operator: Redirect to catalog else Input is invalid Controller-->>Operator: Return form with validation errors end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Catalog items require a name and a valid price; price and stock fields have range/format validation in the model.
  • Items reference one brand and one product type; the EF mappings persist these relationships.
  • Database-backed create operations generate catalog item IDs through the hi-lo sequence helper; the mock service assigns the next ID from the current list.
  • Catalog reads are ordered by item ID and paginated using the supplied page size and index.
  • MVC form submissions use anti-forgery validation; no role-based or resource-ownership checks were found.
  • Database changes are saved through the EF context. No cross-service transaction, saga, or audit trail was identified.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The application targets .NET Framework 4.6.1 and 4.7.2, while the ported app targets net461 and depends on ASP.NET Core 2.2 and EF Core 2.2. These frameworks and packages are out of support. The legacy MVC project declares Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.1, which is affected by CVE-2024-21907; the ported project declares 13.0.2.

Notable Observations

  • Two projects carry different Autofac versions and separate MVC/EF generations.
  • eShopLegacy.Utilities uses BinaryFormatter, which is obsolete in modern .NET.
  • The legacy MVC project declares packages both in its project file and packages.config.

Caching Strategy

No cache provider, cache API, or cache invalidation strategy was found. CatalogServiceMock holds catalog data in memory when mock mode is enabled, but this is the selected data implementation rather than a cache. In both applications the mock service is registered as a singleton and its mutable list is shared across requests.

Data Ownership Boundaries

Each application has its own EF context and connection configuration; neither calls the other or shares data through an API. The logical catalog schema is repeated in both applications. The database-backed service is the source of truth in database mode; the mock service uses preconfigured data when enabled.
